catalog_quote: CHAPTER 1 OUTLINE OF THE MUMUYE PHONOLOGY § 1. The basic elements necessary for the description of Mumuye phonology are: consonant, vowel and tone . They will be symbolized by the third reader, V and T respectively in formulaic expressions . ... § 4. There are three level tones: high, mid and low . ... accent mark (à); the mid tone will be left unmarked (a), or marked a if necessary . A tone mark without a vowel represents a non - seg- mental tone, which is realized on the preceding vowel [p.1] ... § 62. Three phonologically significant pitch levels can be distinguished in the pronunciation of a syllable . They are the high, mid and low tone levels . Some sets of lexical items which are entirely, or almost entirely, distinguished by tone are listed below . [p.15] ... This segment carries a tone . By placing the optional elements in parentheses, the four structures can summarized in a formula as follows: T (C1) V (C2) where C1 is any of the consonant segments, V is any of the six vowels, or [p.19] ... tones, which are contracted into a falling tone, is deleted, v . § 309: # kpáà wu › kpå wu (not ' kpá` wu) ' meet him ' . ... § 82. Tonal assimilation (frequent but optional) Both the high and the low tone, i.e. the marked tones, have assimilatory influence over the preceding tone within a word . [p.24]

The high tone will be marked, normally over a vowel, with an acute accent mark (ex. á), and the low tone with a grave accent mark (à); the mid tone will be left unmarked [...] (p.1) — CHAPTER 5 TONE SYSTEM § 62. Three phonologically significant pitch levels can be distinguished in the pronunciation of a syllable. They are the high, mid and low tone levels. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mumuye (Zing) is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L; plus floating/grammatical tones and contracted falling tones); every syllable nucleus bears a tone. The grammar's phonology (chapters 1-7) contains no statement about word stress or accent: the words 'stress', 'stressed', 'intonation', 'rhythm', 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the book per Google Books full-text search, and 'accent' occurs only in 'accent mark' for tone diacritics.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes seen: disyllabic verb stems carry the same tone on both syllables (p.61); identical adjacent tones contract, marked (H, L) tones assimilate preceding tones within a word (pp.23-24).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone-bearing unit = syllable nucleus (vowel or syllabic nasal); lexical and grammatical (floating) tone. A second-hand areal survey (Hyman et al. 2020, OHLP Table 12.2) cites Mumuye (Shimizu 1983) for 'stem-initial prominence marked by distributional asymmetries', which is positional prominence of the stem-initial syllable, not a stress rule. Access caveat: the Shimizu text was verified only through Google Books search-within-volume snippets and hit counts, not by reading the pages.
new_statements.identity_note: The primary description (Shimizu 1983) is explicitly of the Zing dialect of Mumuye (Glottolog dialect zinn1239 under nucl1240), data collected at Zing 1973. Shimizu 1979 covers the dialect cluster comparatively (Proto-Mumuye tone reconstruction).

new_statements.quote: Mumuye has a three-level tone system with three register tones and a few glides. More study on tone has to be done. Grammatical tone is found on verbs and dominates the tense system. On pronouns, high tone marks imperative.

Krüsi independently (fieldwork 1968-1972, Lankaviri) gives a three-register-tone system and is likewise silent on stress. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mumuye (Lankaviri area, where Krüsi worked from 1968) is described as a tone language with three register tones (plus a few glides) and grammatical tone on verbs and pronouns; the paper says nothing about word stress, so no stress placement can be drawn from it.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress discussion); tonal detail only: grammatical tone on verbs dominates the tense system; high tone on pronouns marks imperative.
new_statements.identity_note: Krüsi's data are from Lankaviri (fieldwork begun 1968, paper written at a 1972 SIL workshop in Nigeria), i.e. the Lankaviri-area Mumuye of the SIL programme; the catalog source Shimizu 1983 describes the Zing dialect. Both are Nuclear Mumuye (nucl1240); the tonal typing is the same in both.
